newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan controllers ignore order to resume work.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan controllers ignore order to resume work.

text.p: Airlines cancelled flights on Wednesday as Kenyan air traffic controllers ignored a government order to resume work and stuck to a go-slow for a fifth day.
"The go-slow is still on but things appear to have improved. We are moving much faster," said an official at national carrier Kenya Airways, worst affected by the go-slow action.
Airports at Nairobi, the coast city of Mombasa, Kisumu and the tourist resort of Malindi were hit hard by the dispute.
Air traffic controllers are demanding a 50-fold increase from what they say is pay of about $90 a month, plus benefits.
Gulf Air was forced to cancel its weekly flight to Uganda via Nairobi from Muscat. A Gulf Air official said it would fly only to Nairobi and back to Muscat until further notice.

Lufthansa Cargo said it was considering cancelling a Boeing 747 from Nairobi on Friday amid "serious concerns" over air safety because of the go-slow and a general strike called for Friday by an opposition-backed alliance.
David Keary, general manager for East and Central Africa for Lufthansa Cargo, said he estimated total losses from the cargo load scheduled for Friday to be worth about $400,000.

Freddy Ganz, Jomo Kenyatta International Airport station manager for Swissair, Royal Dutch Airlines KLM and Sabena, told Reuters his flights were "heavily delayed" -- normally one hour on arrival and departure.
"Passengers are very upset, they are furious," Ganz said.
He said the go-slow meant losses for airlines on account of passengers missing connections, accommodation and waiting. He also spoke of extra cost in fuel and environmental impacts.
Ganz, like Lufthansa, raised concerns about safety.

"There is a definite concern about safety. We have our concerns that the ATCs (Air Traffic Controllers) can handle this kind of operation," said Ganz, adding that the international air travel agency IATA was also worried about safety over Kenya.
The go-slow increased pressure on a government hit by the International Monetary Fund on Thursday halting a $205 million aid package to Kenya, citing concern at high-level corruption.
Labour Minister Philip Masinde late on Tuesday declared the go-slow "unlawful" and directed the controllers to resume work.

Fares Kuindwa, head of the civil service and secretary to the cabinet, visited controllers at the Jomo Kenyatta Airport in Nairobi on Tuesday and told the controllers that the government was examining their demands but that meantime they must resume work.

Keary said Friday's cargo shipment of between 60 and 70 tonnes consisted of cut flowers, vegetables and fresh fish for European markets and unless urgent improvements took place at Nairobi airport Lufthansa would be forced to cancel the flight.

Meanwhile Airlink, an 85 percent-owned subsidiary of Swiss freight forwarder giant Kuehne & Nagel, said it was forced to write off some two tonnes of fresh cut flowers for destinations in Taiwan and Australia.
Kenya produced more than 90,000 tonnes of cut flowers, fruits and vegetables in 1996. Ninety percent were exported by air.

Another major freight forwarder, who asked not to be named, said his company had a whole Boeing 747 freighter of flowers which, because of the delays, had been re-routed from Amsterdam to Luxembourg and now would miss a flower auction in Holland.
